items.title: [theguardian.com] Gisèle Pelicot to sue publisher over unauthorized nude photos
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Gisèle Pelicot said she would take legal action against French publisher Tinbad and psychoanalyst Sabine Prokhoris after nude photographs of her were used without her consent to promote Prokhoris’ essay on coercive control. The images, taken by her former husband, were sent to some media outlets to publicize the book. Pelicot said she was “deeply shocked” and refused to let her private life become an advertising tool. Tinbad apologized for what it called an “unfortunate communication error” and said it had not sent images of rape or pornographic videos. It did not deny distributing nude photographs. Prokhoris said the publisher bore full responsibility for the campaign and described her book as a critical examination of psychological control, not a study of the Pelicot case. The essay includes a chapter on the case, and its back-cover text describes coercive control as a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy. Tinbad said it would stop promoting the book and print no additional copies beyond the 280 already in circulation. Pelicot’s lawyer, Christophe Bigot, said the book challenges her status as a victim.

items.title: [bbc.com] Brazil activates protective measures after about 20 isolated Awá approach
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

items.title: [elpais.com] Journalist's murder in Costa Rica raises alarm among regional press
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri was shot dead on November 16, three days after an unknown person set fire to two cars and part of the home of Panamanian investigative journalist Rolando Rodríguez in Panama City. Following the killing in Santo Domingo de Heredia, Costa Rica, press organizations and the United Nations called for an investigation and warned of its chilling effect on journalism. Reporters Without Borders (RSF), an international organization that defends press freedom, said it had already raised the alarm about pressure on critical journalists and obstacles to reporting independently. A University of Costa Rica poll published on November 11 found that 58% of the population considers journalism dangerous to practice, and 54.7% believes freedom of expression is at risk. The Costa Rican Prosecutor's Office said it would examine Rodríguez's public allegations, the people he named, and other possible motives for the crime. items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Developer Cody Collier has released NO SPEAKER, a free, open-source tool that makes a MacBook’s Force Touch trackpad produce speech, tones and simple music through its haptic motor, even with the laptop’s speakers muted. The software drives the motor fast enough to make the glass surface vibrate audibly. It cannot play sound from other apps, and its output is quiet and robotic. NO SPEAKER uses a private, undocumented macOS framework to control the motor, so an Apple software update could break compatibility. Collier says the tool stays within the motor’s normal maximum strength, but the effect of prolonged use on trackpad life is unknown. The project is available on GitHub; Collier has tested it on only a small number of Mac models.

items.title: [space.com] Apollo 12 lightning strikes prompted NASA to tighten launch weather rules
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Lightning struck NASA’s Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket twice within seconds of its Nov. 14, 1969, launch, disrupting spacecraft telemetry and endangering the mission. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized the readings from an earlier test and recommended switching the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary setting, which restored the data. Investigators concluded the rocket and its conductive exhaust plume had triggered a discharge in an electrically charged part of the atmosphere, even though no active thunderstorm lay along the immediate flight path. NASA expanded launch weather restrictions to account for atmospheric electrical conditions, not only visible lightning and thunderstorms.

Quebec Superior Court Justice Ian Demers suspended the province’s 2022 exemption from the Crown oath required of lawmakers across Canada, saying Quebec could not change the constitutional requirement on its own. Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he will appeal. The dispute could affect the legal standing of legislation passed by Quebec’s newly elected assembly, while the underlying challenge has yet to be heard on its merits. Ottawa lawyer Lawrence David, who brought the case, says the oath requirement applies to the King as Canada’s head of state. Laval University constitutional law professor Patrick Taillon argues that courts could temporarily preserve laws later found invalid, citing a Supreme Court remedy in a Manitoba language case. Quebec’s legislature is scheduled to resume Dec. 1.

The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor and posted a notice for users on the Academy website rather than emailing them individually.

Released by the conference presidency on Nov. 16, the text remains under negotiation and does not represent an agreed position; the talks in Antalya, Türkiye, are scheduled to end Nov. 20. The United Nations Environment Programme estimates developing countries will need $305 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, while international public adaptation finance reached $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024. Ghanaian Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings also called for funding to restore land and rivers damaged by mining and for greater local processing of Africa’s minerals.

Authorities and specialists recommend screening tests, clinical follow-up, and sustained lifestyle changes. He also noted that 36.9% of the planned rural development programs have been completed.

items.title: [politico.eu] Germany's conservatives back Bavarian speaker Ilse Aigner as first woman president
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative bloc has agreed to back Bavarian parliament speaker Ilse Aigner to succeed German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, potentially making her the first woman to hold the largely ceremonial office. Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is expected to formally endorse her at leadership meetings on Monday, Nov. 9; the Federal Convention is scheduled to elect Steinmeier’s successor on Jan. 30, 2027. Aigner, 61, belongs to the Christian Social Union (CSU), the CDU’s Bavarian sister party. The CSU put her forward earlier this year, but Merz delayed backing her while considering alternatives, including Bundestag President Julia Klöckner. Support from Social Democrats and Greens, as well as CDU state leaders, grew in recent weeks. The choice followed weeks of tension between the CDU and CSU over whom to nominate. Steinmeier’s second five-year term ends in March 2027, and he cannot seek another term. Germany’s president represents the country and signs legislation, while the chancellor leads the government. Every president since the Federal Republic’s founding in 1949 has been a man.

The regulator’s order also requires the company to change the tool to provide relevant data and identify information it cannot supply for privacy reasons.

Governments and regulators are reassessing privacy safeguards, with Finland reviewing rules governing workplace communications, Hong Kong launching a support program for organisations adopting artificial intelligence, and European lawmakers debating proposed changes to data-protection law. Finland is seeking views before deciding whether to pursue legislation, Hong Kong is offering training and surveying business practices, and European Union lawmakers and privacy specialists are disputing whether proposed simplifications would weaken protections. The review is preparatory only; comments are due Dec. 6, 2026, and the ministry plans to publish its completed memorandum by year-end. Hong Kong’s first initiative will offer three free data-security seminars for small businesses and NGOs; its AI and Data Privacy Survey 2026 is expected later this year.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Earth’s energy imbalance has reached its highest level since monitoring began, and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Global surface temperature averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level from January through September; a developing, unusually strong El Niño could push the annual figure higher and prolong extreme heat into 2027. The agency released its report as the U.N. climate summit COP31 opened in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiations scheduled through Nov. 20. The agency says each of the past 12 years ranked among the 12 warmest on record, with 2023-2026 likely to be the four warmest years. Greenhouse gases from human activity are trapping heat; the ocean absorbs about 90% of the excess, while sea levels and ocean temperatures have reached records. The WMO warns that the accumulating heat will intensify heat waves, droughts, tropical cyclones and heavy rain. A separate U.N. Environment Programme assessment says warming will exceed 1.5°C under every plausible emissions pathway. Returning below that threshold this century would require near-zero emissions and the removal of hundreds of billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide. The WMO’s full 2026 climate report is due in March 2027.

items.title: [medicalxpress.com] Brazilian study finds genetic tests for heart failure less accurate
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A University of São Paulo study found that genetic tests used to investigate heart failure are less accurate for Brazilians, particularly when DNA segments reflect African or Indigenous ancestry, because these groups are underrepresented in genomic research and databases. Researchers analyzed genomes from 1,013 patients at São Paulo’s Heart Institute: 77.7% had at least one genetic variant whose effect on the disease remains uncertain. Genetic results can help assess a patient’s prognosis and tailor treatment, and can guide screening of relatives when a disease-causing variant is identified. The researchers said more Brazilian genetic research and public data infrastructure are needed to improve interpretation. The study was published in August in JACC: Advances.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A major international study tracking more than 26,000 men found that very low testosterone levels were associated with an 18% higher risk of dying from cancer later in life. Surprisingly, testosterone itself showed no clear link to prostate cancer, although two other sex hormones did. Researchers believe low testosterone could be an important early warning sign of future health risks, particularly when levels fall below 8.6 nmol/L.

items.title: [therecord.media] FBI investigates reported breach of national crime database
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The FBI is investigating a reported intrusion into its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a law-enforcement database used to check records on warrants, missing people and stolen property. Investigators have not said who accessed it or what data, if any, was taken. CNN first reported the breach on Nov. 20, citing two people briefed on the investigation, and the FBI has not publicly confirmed it. President Donald Trump acknowledged the incident in a Nov. 21 interview, calling it “not good” and suggesting the intrusion could expose investigative files. The breach would be the second reported FBI cybersecurity incident in about two months, following a September intrusion into the bureau’s job site. The scope remains unclear, and a cybersecurity executive said investigators should determine whether attackers altered or deleted records, not just whether they stole information.

items.title: [cyberscoop.com] Kazakh ransomware suspect extradited to US in healthcare extortion case
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Kazakh national Roman Khlynovskiy, 43, was extradited from Italy and appeared in federal court in Knoxville, Tennessee, on charges related to alleged ransomware attacks on U.S. hospitals, schools and healthcare providers. Prosecutors say he was part of the 8-Digits Team, a group linked to the INC and Lynx ransomware operations that breached networks, stole data and demanded payment not to publish it. The indictment says the group claimed to possess more than 50 terabytes of stolen data, including over 70 million confidential health records, and issued ransom demands totaling more than $500 million. Khlynovskiy faces charges including computer fraud, wire fraud, extortion and money laundering, as well as threats involving nonconsensual intimate images under the TAKE IT DOWN Act. If convicted on all charges, he could face up to 27 years in prison. The FBI said its investigation is continuing.

items.title: [theregister.com] Web-testing platform Optimizely breach exposes visitors at 178 sites to malware
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Hackers exploited a vulnerability in website-testing platform Optimizely on Nov. 16, injecting malicious JavaScript into scripts used by 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, IKEA, HSBC and Salesforce. Security researcher Scott Helme and cybersecurity firm Report URI found that the code reached visitors through Optimizely’s trusted delivery infrastructure, without requiring attackers to break into each customer’s servers. The scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, capture card details entered into website forms, steal browser cookies, take screenshots and load exploit kits targeting older Apple iPhones and iPads. Report URI tracked about $7,040 in cryptocurrency sent to attacker-linked wallets in roughly nine hours. Researchers could not establish how many card details were stolen and reported no confirmed iPhone takeover in this campaign. Optimizely said it patched the flaw, removed the injected code, revoked tokens and reset access for affected accounts. Salesforce disabled the scripts while investigating, and IKEA opened an inquiry. Equifax stopped using the service and said it found no evidence its systems were compromised.

Israel struck a mountainous area near Janta in eastern Lebanon on Monday, Nov. 16, saying it targeted a weapons shipment sent from Syria for Hezbollah. Lebanon’s National News Agency reported that the strike hit the Al-Shaara area at dawn and caused no casualties or damage. The Israeli military also said it detained two men in southern Lebanon whom it described as Hezbollah-guided operatives; Lebanese state media said Israeli forces seized two brothers in Shebaa. A U.S.-backed framework for Lebanon calls for Hezbollah’s disarmament, an Israeli troop withdrawal and Lebanese army deployment in the south, but implementation has stalled and Hezbollah has rejected surrendering its weapons. Haaretz described the attack as a departure from Israel’s prolonged restraint on strikes deep inside Lebanon. Israeli forces continue operating in a self-declared security zone along the border.
